story.title: How I got here
story.paragraph1: I graduated with a commerce degree, then taught myself frontend three years ago through online courses: JavaScript, HTML and CSS, then React, Next.js and Tailwind CSS. I later spent three months as a trainee at a software company, building a real survey product rather than a demo. There I learned Git and GitHub, clean architecture, clean code, and how to work with a real API.
story.paragraph2: AI is reshaping the market, so I've started studying AI automation and will begin a dedicated course next month. The goal is to fold it into how I build, while keeping every AI-generated output reviewed by a human before it ships.

real-estate-hub.overview: A multi-region property marketplace built with a small team. I owned the Buy and Rent pages end to end — from the listing grid to search, filtering and sorting.
real-estate-hub.problem: The team needed working Buy/Rent pages before the real backend was ready, so the UI had to be built against a mock API and still feel production-ready.
goals: Ship a listing grid that reads real data, not static cards
Support search, filter and sort without a page reload
Keep pagination usable on both desktop and mobile

approach.title: Mock the API first
approach.text: Modeled property data behind a local REST layer (query params for status, sort and pagination) so the UI could be built and tested before the real backend existed.

approach.title: Centralize fetch state
approach.text: Used TanStack Query to handle loading, caching and refetching whenever a filter or sort option changed, instead of managing that by hand.

features.title: Search and filtering
features.text: Filter by location, price, property type, bedrooms and bathrooms, combined into a single query.

features.title: Sorting
features.text: Sort by price (low/high), area or newest, applied through the same query.

features.title: Responsive pagination
features.text: Page-based navigation on larger screens, infinite scroll on mobile.

design.pointText: The listing grid had to stay scannable at any screen size, so card density and image ratio were tuned before any detail-page work started.

implementation.title: Data fetching
implementation.text: React with TanStack Query and Context API for shared filter state across the Buy and Rent pages.

implementation.title: UI layer
implementation.text: Tailwind CSS for layout, MUI for form controls, Framer Motion for card and filter transitions.

challenges.pointTitle: Keeping filters, sort and pagination in sync
challenges.pointText: All three had to update the same query without racing each other or losing the current page when a filter changed — solved by driving everything off one query key derived from the active filters.

detail.caption: The Buy page across desktop, tablet and mobile.

renova.overview: A responsive e-commerce storefront built from scratch in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with real product data and full Arabic/English support.
renova.problem: Most e-commerce practice projects stop at static markup. This one needed to actually fetch and render product data, and work in two languages and directions.
goals: Render real product data instead of hardcoded cards
Support category browsing and a working cart
Ship a bilingual UI (Arabic and English) without duplicating markup

approach.title: API first, layout second
approach.text: Wired up the product API calls before finishing the visual design, so the layout was built against real data shapes from the start.

approach.title: One markup, two languages
approach.text: Structured the JavaScript to swap text and direction (LTR/RTL) from a single source of truth, instead of maintaining two separate pages.

features.title: Dynamic product listing
features.text: Products, categories and pricing pulled live from an API and rendered client-side.

features.title: Cart
features.text: Add, update and remove items with totals recalculated in real time.

features.title: Language switch
features.text: Full Arabic/English toggle, including layout direction, from one codebase.

design.pointText: Layout and touch targets were designed for small screens first, then expanded up — not the other way around.

implementation.title: No framework
implementation.text: Built in vanilla JavaScript to practice DOM manipulation and async data flow without relying on framework state management.

implementation.title: Async data
implementation.text: All product and category data loaded asynchronously, with loading and empty states handled explicitly.

challenges.pointText: Switching between Arabic and English meant flipping the whole layout direction, not just translating strings — handled by keeping spacing and alignment logical (start/end) rather than hardcoded left/right.

detail.caption: The storefront across desktop, tablet and mobile.

dolistix.overview: A task manager built to go past basic to-do apps — categorized tasks, due dates, priorities, fuzzy search and drag-and-drop, all running client-side.
dolistix.problem: Simple to-do lists don't test much. This one needed real interaction complexity: search that tolerates typos, reordering by drag, and state that survives a refresh.
goals: Persist tasks without a backend
Make search forgiving, not just exact-match
Support editing, completion and due dates per task

approach.title: localStorage as the data layer
approach.text: All tasks, categories and completion state are persisted to localStorage, so the app works fully offline with no server.

approach.title: Fuzzy search from the start
approach.text: Integrated Fuse.js early so search behaves like a real product feature, not an afterthought exact-match filter.

features.title: Category tabs
features.text: Tasks grouped into All, Personal, Work, Study and custom categories, filterable from the top nav.

features.title: Fuzzy search
features.text: Typo-tolerant search across task titles, powered by Fuse.js.

features.title: Drag-and-drop and dark mode
features.text: Reorder tasks by dragging, and switch themes without losing state.

design.pointTitle: Status grouping over a flat list
design.pointText: Tasks are split into Today, Other, Completed and Incomplete groups instead of one long list, so priority is visible without opening anything.

implementation.title: Forms and validation
implementation.text: Formik and Yup handle the task and login forms, including due-date and required-field validation.

implementation.title: Stable identity
implementation.text: uuid generates unique ids per task so drag-and-drop reordering and edits never collide.

challenges.pointTitle: State that survives without a backend
challenges.pointText: Every mutation (add, edit, complete, reorder) has to stay in sync with localStorage immediately, with no server as a source of truth to fall back on.

detail.caption: The task list across desktop, tablet and mobile.

user-dashboard.overview: An Arabic-first admin panel for managing users — full CRUD, live pagination and instant light/dark switching, built on Next.js App Router.
user-dashboard.problem: Admin panels are usually English-only and single-theme by default. This one needed to be genuinely RTL and support both light and dark themes from the first screen.
goals: Full CRUD on users: create, read, update, delete
Paginated, sortable data instead of one long table
A real RTL layout, not a mirrored English one

approach.title: Server state via TanStack Query
approach.text: Every list, create, update and delete action goes through TanStack Query, so the table stays in sync after any mutation without manual refetch logic.

approach.title: RTL as the default, not an override
approach.text: Built the layout in Arabic first, so spacing, icons and alignment were correct by default instead of patched in afterwards.

features.title: User CRUD
features.text: Create, view, update and delete users from color-coded action cards.

features.title: Paginated table
features.text: Users list paginated against the API, with total count read from response headers.

features.title: Theme toggle
features.text: Instant light/dark switching with no layout shift or flash.

design.pointText: Each core action (create, read, update, delete) gets its own accent color, so the dashboard is scannable at a glance instead of relying on labels alone.

implementation.title: Data layer
implementation.text: Axios client with a typed API layer, paginated through query params and the response's total-count header.

implementation.title: App structure
implementation.text: Next.js App Router with TypeScript, organized by feature (a users module) rather than by file type.

challenges.pointTitle: Keeping the table in sync after every mutation
challenges.pointText: Create, update and delete all needed to invalidate the same paginated query without a full page reload or a stale row lingering in the table.

detail.caption: The dashboard across desktop, tablet and mobile.

dashboard.overview: A responsive admin dashboard shell — sidebar navigation, stat cards and activity widgets — built as a clean starting point for wiring up real data.
dashboard.problem: Most dashboard templates online are either bloated with a framework or too rigid to extend. This one needed to be plain, readable HTML/CSS/JS that's easy to build on.
goals: A sidebar layout that holds up on smaller screens
Reusable stat-card and widget patterns
No framework dependency to get in the way

approach.title: Layout first
approach.text: Built the sidebar-plus-content shell before any widget, so every screen after that just slots into an already-responsive frame.

approach.title: Componentized CSS
approach.text: Wrote each widget (stat card, ticket list, task list) as an isolated, reusable block instead of one long stylesheet.

features.title: Stat cards
features.text: At-a-glance metrics (tickets, targets) with a consistent card pattern.

features.title: Activity widgets
features.text: Latest news and latest tasks panels, ready to bind to real data.

features.title: Sidebar navigation
features.text: Collapsible sidebar with icon-based navigation.

design.pointText: The template intentionally leans on layout and hierarchy rather than heavy visual styling, so it's easy to reskin for a real product.

implementation.title: No build step
implementation.text: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no bundler, so the whole thing runs from static files.

implementation.title: Grid-based layout
implementation.text: CSS Grid for the dashboard shell, keeping the sidebar and content areas independently scrollable.

challenges.pointTitle: A sidebar that doesn't break on small screens
challenges.pointText: Getting the fixed sidebar to collapse cleanly on mobile without heavy JavaScript breakpoint logic took a few iterations on the CSS Grid structure.

detail.caption: The dashboard shell across desktop, tablet and mobile.

kasper.overview: A dark, editorial-style landing template built section by section — hero, services, portfolio, pricing and contact — in semantic HTML and hand-written CSS.
kasper.problem: The goal was to practice building a full multi-section marketing site from a static design, without a CSS framework to lean on.
goals: Match a multi-section layout closely from a design reference
Keep every section responsive without a framework
Add motion (slider, hover effects) without a JS library

approach.title: Section by section
approach.text: Built and tested each section (hero, services, portfolio, pricing, contact) independently before assembling the full page.

approach.title: Custom slider logic
approach.text: Wrote the hero image slider and navigation dots in plain JavaScript instead of pulling in a carousel library.

features.title: Hero slider
features.text: Auto-advancing hero with manual prev/next controls and dot indicators.

features.title: Section navigation
features.text: Smooth-scrolling nav links between Services, Portfolio, About, Pricing and Contact.

features.title: Image overlays
features.text: Hover overlays on portfolio and service images for a more editorial feel.

design.pointText: The hero leans on a full-bleed photograph with a translucent text panel, rather than flat color, to set an editorial tone from the first screen.

implementation.title: Semantic HTML
implementation.text: Sections use proper landmark elements (nav, section, footer) instead of generic divs throughout.

implementation.title: Organized CSS3
implementation.text: One stylesheet per concern (layout, components, sections) instead of a single global file.

challenges.pointText: Getting the in-page nav links to scroll to the right offset — accounting for the fixed header — took some manual scroll-position math.

detail.caption: The template across desktop, tablet and mobile.

elzero.overview: A services-and-testimonials landing page built to practice clean, organized CSS3 and semantic HTML — animated counters included.
elzero.problem: The exercise was specifically about CSS discipline: writing a full page's styles in a way that stays readable and maintainable, not just working.
goals: Organize CSS by section instead of one flat file
Animate counters and elements without a JS animation library
Keep the markup semantic throughout

approach.title: Plan the sections first
approach.text: Sketched out services, testimonials and counters as separate blocks before writing any CSS, to keep each one self-contained.

approach.title: CSS-driven animation
approach.text: Used CSS transitions and keyframes for hover and reveal effects instead of a JavaScript animation library.

features.title: Services section
features.text: Icon-led service cards in a responsive grid.

features.title: Testimonials
features.text: Customer quote cards with a consistent layout.

features.title: Animated counters
features.text: Numbers that count up into view as the user scrolls.

design.pointText: Every section reuses the same spacing scale and card pattern, so the page reads as one system rather than a collection of separate experiments.

implementation.title: Semantic structure
implementation.text: Proper heading hierarchy and landmark elements throughout, not just visual formatting.

implementation.title: Organized CSS3
implementation.text: Styles grouped by section with consistent naming, making the stylesheet easy to navigate.

challenges.pointTitle: Counters that only animate once, on view
challenges.pointText: Triggering the counter animation exactly when it scrolls into view — and not re-triggering it on every scroll — needed a simple visibility check rather than a scroll-position listener.

detail.caption: The page across desktop, tablet and mobile.

leno.overview: A one-page landing template focused on layout animation and a tight mobile-first build, in HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript.
leno.problem: The brief was a single, self-contained landing page — everything had to live in one scroll, with no routing or multiple views.
goals: Keep the entire experience on one page
Animate sections in as the user scrolls
Build mobile-first, not desktop-first

approach.title: Mobile layout first
approach.text: Built and styled the small-screen layout before expanding up to tablet and desktop breakpoints.

approach.title: Scroll-triggered animation
approach.text: Sections fade and slide into view on scroll, using lightweight JavaScript rather than a heavier animation library.

features.title: Single-page flow
features.text: All sections (hero, about, features, contact) live on one scrollable page.

features.title: Scroll animations
features.text: Layout elements animate in as they enter the viewport.

features.title: Clean, minimal structure
features.text: A deliberately small codebase kept easy to read end to end.

design.pointText: Section spacing and typography scale were kept consistent throughout, so scrolling through the page feels like one continuous read rather than stitched-together blocks.

implementation.title: Vanilla JavaScript
implementation.text: No framework or animation library — scroll listeners and class toggles drive the reveal animations.

implementation.title: Mobile-first CSS
implementation.text: Base styles target small screens, with breakpoints layered on top for tablet and desktop.

challenges.pointText: Running animation checks on every scroll event risked jank on lower-end devices, so the scroll listener was throttled to keep it smooth.

detail.caption: The landing page across desktop, tablet and mobile.
